title: Design a multicast feed handler with gap recovery
question: Design a low-latency market-data feed handler for a multicast exchange feed, including gap detection, recovery, and downstream publication.
clarifyingQuestions: What is the expected message rate and burst profile?
Do we have snapshot and retransmit channels in addition to multicast?
interviewerIntent: Evaluating end-to-end low-latency architecture
Evaluating correctness under packet loss and operational failure
answerOutline: Define venue protocol assumptions and latency budget
Separate packet capture, decode, sequencing, book-apply, and publish stages
Track sequence numbers per channel and instrument group
Use bounded buffering plus replay or snapshot recovery
Keep the hot path single-writer where possible
Design active-active redundancy across hosts and NICs
Expose health, gap, and latency telemetry
Provide deterministic replay for testing and postmortems
sampleAnswer: I would start by fixing the correctness contract: downstream consumers must never confuse missing data with fresh data, so the handler needs explicit stale-state semantics in addition to raw speed. The hot path should be split into capture, decode, sequencing, book-apply, and publish, with minimal copying and a single-writer model per shard so the common case avoids locks and ambiguous ownership. A sequencer per channel detects gaps, duplicates, and unexpected resets; on a gap, it buffers a bounded window of later packets, requests retransmission or snapshot recovery, and decides whether downstream publication can continue or must be marked stale. For resilience, I would run active-active handlers on separate hosts or NIC paths, keep sequence and health telemetry visible, and make failover explicit rather than relying on a silent winner-takes-all race that is hard to debug. Operationally, I want wire-to-app latency histograms, gap rates, recovery success, decode errors, backlog depth, and per-stage timing so production issues can be localized quickly. Finally, I would insist on deterministic replay from packet captures because feed handlers are hard to reason about from logs alone and regression testing is essential once venue quirks and edge cases accumulate.
commonMistakes: Focusing only on parsing speed and skipping recovery logic
Publishing partial book state while a gap is unresolved
followUps: How would you shard by channel or instrument?
What changes if the venue provides only snapshots and no retransmit?
seniorExtension: Discuss how you would support multiple venues with heterogeneous protocols while keeping the hot path efficient and the normalization layer testable.

I would store enough event history to replay every failover decision, because these systems are often debugged after the fact when the immediate symptoms are gone. The core tradeoff is between seamlessness and explainability, and I would bias toward a design that operators and strategy teams can reason about under stress.

If order-level cancellation is required, I also need an ID lookup table pointing to the owning price level entry so deletes do not degenerate into scans. Sequence handling stays outside but adjacent to the book: the book should never apply out-of-order or gap-affected updates without explicit stale semantics, otherwise the data structure can be fast and still wrong. Derived metrics such as imbalance or custom views should usually subscribe to book-change events instead of living inside the core mutation path, which keeps the hot loop tight and easier to reason about. Finally, I want deterministic snapshot and replay support so I can prove correctness under venue edge cases and benchmark real update distributions rather than synthetic happy paths.

Replay is powerful because I can validate both the book and analytics against historical events and ensure derived values remain consistent after implementation changes. The architecture would separate strategy ingress, pre-trade checks, routing, venue-session handling, and authoritative state tracking, with each order shard owned by one thread or partition to avoid cross-thread mutation races. Every order needs stable internal IDs plus mapping to venue IDs, and all externally significant transitions should be journaled or at least durably sequenced so recovery and post-trade audit are possible. Risk and routing must be designed so the hot path stays deterministic, while slower activities like persistence fan-out, analytics, and client reporting consume transition events asynchronously. I would also define session-reset behavior up front: how unknown in-flight orders are reconciled, how idempotent resends work, and when the system enters a protective degraded mode instead of guessing state. The key is building an OMS that is both fast enough for live routing and disciplined enough to recover and explain every state transition afterward.

Because duplicates can become financial rather than merely technical bugs, I would bias the design toward explicit state and replayability even if that costs some complexity. title: Design incident response and rollback mechanisms
question: How would you design deployment, rollback, and incident-response mechanisms for a latency-sensitive production trading platform?
clarifyingQuestions: Are deployments centralized, per-service, or per-venue component?

sampleAnswer: For latency-sensitive systems I want deployment safety built into the platform, not improvised during incidents, so staged rollout and canaries are the default rather than the exception. Each component should have explicit rollback criteria tied to its real failure modes—latency regression, reject spikes, feed gaps, or session instability—not just generic health checks. I prefer a deployment model where binaries, configs, and feature flags are independently visible and reversible, because mixed hidden state is a common reason rollbacks fail under pressure. During incidents, operators need dependency-aware dashboards and clear ownership maps so they can isolate whether the problem is in market data, strategy, risk, or venue gateways instead of flooding every team at once. Post-incident, the platform should retain enough timelines, configuration versions, and replay inputs that the root cause can be reconstructed without guesswork. The design goal is to make the safe action easy when time pressure is highest.

Treating rollback as simply redeploying old code without considering config and state

title: Design capacity planning and performance regression detection
question: How would you design capacity planning and performance regression detection for a trading platform that experiences bursty market conditions?
clarifyingQuestions: Do you have realistic historical traffic captures for stressful periods?
interviewerIntent: Evaluating forward-looking operational design
Evaluating whether the candidate plans for tails and bursts instead of average load
answerOutline: Define capacity in terms of latency and correctness, not only throughput
Use historical burst replays and synthetic worst cases
Track headroom per stage and per resource domain
Automate regression detection against baselines
Feed findings back into rollout gates and hardware planning
Model venue or market-event specific stress patterns
sampleAnswer: I define capacity as the point where the platform can still meet latency and correctness goals under stressful traffic, not merely the point where it has not crashed. To plan for that, I use historical captures from volatile sessions plus synthetic worst-case bursts so we understand queue growth, recovery behavior, and tail latency before the real market day arrives. Headroom needs to be tracked per stage and per resource domain—CPU, memory bandwidth, NIC queues, exchange throttles, and downstream consumers—because the first bottleneck is rarely the same across all conditions. I would automate regression detection against baseline runs so new code, new configs, or even new hardware microcode cannot drift into production unnoticed. Those results should feed rollout gates and hardware planning, otherwise load tests become ceremonial and disconnected from operational decisions. The strong design plans for burst behavior explicitly because that is where trading systems earn or lose trust.
commonMistakes: Planning capacity on average message rates only
Treating performance testing as an occasional manual exercise
followUps: What signals indicate you are nearing unsafe capacity?
How do you keep replay baselines representative over time?
seniorExtension: Discuss how you would decide between software optimization, topology changes, or new hardware when capacity margins start shrinking.
